title: What is compassion connected to, and does it differ by gender and age?​ ​​A network analysis of compassion, self-compassion, mindfulness, empathy and mental health
Weaving the path towards profitability at Utkalamrita
abstract: Learning outcomes By the end of this case study, learners should be able to: 1. Identify the key managerial, financial and market challenges faced by Utkalamrita brand; 2. Classify cost, prepare cost sheet, conduct common-size analysis, calculate contribution margin and analyse profitability position; 3. Formulate short-term and long-term strategic initiatives to protect contribution margin and move towards profitability target; and 4. Evaluate the financial impact of external policy shocks on exports and profitability. Case overview/synopsis This case examines the costing and profitability challenges faced by handloom entrepreneurs Ms Amrita Sabat and Dr Anita Sabat, co-founders of Utkalamrita, a brand producing Geographical Indication tagged Utkala-Gouraba sarees originating from Odisha, India. While the brand derived cultural value from authentic craftsmanship, fair artisan wages and heritage preservation, these very commitments contributed to a high-cost base and limited pricing flexibility. Operating with low margins, the firm now targeted 12% profitability. A sudden US$100 export duty announcement on all US-bound parcels, effective immediately, eliminated the duty-free threshold that powered international sales for Utkalamrita. A saree order, ready for dispatch to a US client, suddenly became financially unviable. Barely a week before shipment deadline, Amrita had to decide whether to absorb the duty, pass it on to the client or negotiate middle path. Beyond this single order loomed a deeper question, could Utkalamrita survive, achieve 12% profitability and compete amongst dynamic global trade regulations and policies. This case enables students to prepare a cost sheet, conduct common-size analysis and compute contribution margins. Furthermore, students evaluate the financial implications of absorbing the US$100 duty and passing it on to the client through cost–volume–profit analysis. They also explore short-term and long-term strategic initiatives in the face of external shocks. Ultimately, this case integrates cost and managerial accounting with strategic decision-making, encouraging learners to assess how craft-based enterprises navigate external shocks while preserving financial viability and cultural authenticity. The case is grounded in primary data obtained through founders’ interviews. Complexity academic level The case is suitable for undergraduate (Bachelor of Business Administration) and postgraduate (Master of Business Administration) students: primarily aimed at students learning cost and management accounting course. Subject code CSS 1: Accounting and Finance.

title: Uncrewed aircraft systems for blood transport in Kenya: a facility location, utilization, and cost-efficiency analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) are increasingly promoted to improve access to blood and emergency medical commodities in low-and middle-income countries. However, economic evaluations have mostly focused on aircraft performance, with limited attention to base station placement, utilization, and staffing requirements – key determinants of unit cost given high fixed operating expenses. Moreover, blood and similar commodities can only be administered in facilities that are legally authorized and clinically equipped to manage severe adverse reactions, constraining effective demand. We evaluated how these factors would jointly affect the cost-efficiency of UAS blood transport in Kenya. Methods We conducted a facility location and economic analysis of UAS blood transport under three base station placement scenarios: existing blood bank sites, urban centers (> 30,000 population), and unrestricted village and town locations. We estimated geographic and population-weighted coverage of transfusing hospitals, compared UAS flight times with road travel times within identical service areas, and projected delivery volumes and unit costs using facility catchment populations, utilization assumptions, and staffing models consistent with 24/7 emergency operations. Results Across scenarios, three base stations covered 50% of transfusing hospitals and 60–81% of national blood demand when weighted by population. Seven stations would cover 75% of transfusing facilities, and 93% of population demand, beyond which marginal gains diminished sharply. Mean UAS delivery time was approximately one-third of road travel time, with the largest advantage observed in urban and peri-urban corridors – precisely where straight-line distance alone would suggest UAS offer limited benefit. Estimated annual base station costs were US$61,500 [95% CI $58,200: $106,000], of which staffing accounted for 59%-84% of costs. The estimated UAS transport costs per unit of whole blood transported was $7.59 [95% CI $5.4: $34.22], compared to $0.78[95% CI $0.63: $1.01] for road transport under our base assumptions of three units delivered per flight. Achieving complete geographic coverage would require approximately 28 stations, many operating at low utilization and high cost. Conclusions In Kenya, a small number of well-placed UAS base stations can achieve substantial gains in hospital access and delivery speed relative to road transport, particularly in dense urban and peri-urban corridors. UAS blood transport is most cost-efficient when concentrated in a limited number of high-utilization stations; staffing, rather than aircraft costs, dominates expenditure and explains why expansion into low-demand areas rapidly increases unit costs. These cost-efficiency findings should be weighed alongside access and equity value of UAS in remote areas, which this analysis does not capture.

title: Trust gained, trust lost: how service robot anthropomorphism shapes consumer trust in tight and loose cultures
journal: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
abstract: Purpose This paper aimed to examine the dual pathways through which service-robot (SR) anthropomorphism shapes consumer trust in service robots (CTSR), specifically the positive serial mediating effect of perceived warmth (WA) and perceived competence (CO) and the negative serial mediating effect of perceived identity threat (TH) and discomfort (DI). It further explored cross-cultural differences in consumer attitudes and their underlying reasons from the perspective of cultural tightness-looseness. Design/methodology/approach Five scenario experiments were conducted across three sets of SR picture stimuli, two service settings (hotel and hospital) and two cultures (China and the United States). Findings Both study 1 and study 2 found that anthropomorphism had a double-edged sword effect on CTSR across different sets of SR picture stimuli, service settings and cultures. An exploratory analysis in study 1 further revealed that among Chinese consumers, CTSR and its antecedents did not show significant differences across different service settings. Study 2 results further indicated that Chinese (versus. American) consumers had higher WA, CO and CTSR, along with lower TH and DI and that region-level cultural tightness influenced CTSR and its antecedents, potentially explaining these cross-cultural differences. Practical implications For hospitality managers, this paper offers insights on how to deploy anthropomorphic SRs across different cultural contexts. Originality/value This study developed a dialectical framework that integrates cognitive and affective serial mediation pathways and considers both the country- and region-level effects of cultural tightness on attitudes toward SRs.

title: Toward Ternary Computing Enabled by Origami-Inspired Modular Architectures
abstract: Abstract Modern mechanical computing, being envisioned as a pathway toward structure- and material-level processing, holds potential for intelligent metamaterials and robotics in extreme environments. However, current computing architectures remain constrained by binary paradigms. Here, we introduce an origami-inspired modular architecture that encodes logical mappings into its inherent kinematic responses under an input-output decoupled paradigm, enabling both binary and ternary mechanical computing. Within this emerging paradigm, the multi-stable states of two Kresling origami configurations serve as physical carriers for generating discrete signals, while torsional transitions among these states ensure signal switching, supporting operations from logic gates to advanced arithmetic. Based on this mechanical architecture, we systematically demonstrate seven common logic gates and modular arithmetic half- and full-adders in both binary and ternary systems, revealing challenges and opportunities in advancing multi-valued logic through comparative analysis. The physical platform, along with its accompanying response-programming strategy, represents a simplified and generalized paradigm that supports migration to higher-level mechanical computing mechanisms.

title: The case of PBX operators in a multinational hotel company: job performance and communication
abstract: Purpose Managing All Guest Incoming Calls (MAGIC) is a department in a five-star hotel in Mumbai, India. A couple of PBX operators were hired to work in the MAGIC department. The operators shared a foundational knowledge base, and managed information and guests' requests using improvised solutions. Every call to the PBX operator require equal attention and the same standard of service. Some calls require a “handle with care” status more than others. PBX operators make decisions with the approval of Duty Managers and Front Office Managers. It is important to examine the work design within MAGIC. To support optimal performance, technology and information must be easily accessible, and PBX operators should be regularly updated with current data. The Erlang C model is a popular model used for performance measurement in MAGIC. Design/methodology/approach This case study offers an in-depth, holistic investigation of a real-world phenomenon within its specific operational context. The narrative centers on how the hotel leveraged or failed to leverage—physical assets, staff competencies, and technological resources to maintain a competitive advantage, explicitly grounding its analysis in the technological and economic realities of that time. Findings Within the hotel, communication typically adheres to established chains of command and is formally documented. Vertical communication occurs in two directions: downward and upward. Downward communication flows from managers to staff, for instance, from the general manager (GM) to the front office manager. At MAGIC, human resources (HR) failed to provide continuous training and development, contributing to elevated turnover rates driven by the stressful nature of PBX operations. Additionally, employee job performance and discretion directly impact overall guest service quality. Ultimately, this case study provides practical implications regarding PBX operators-employees frequently overlooked by HR and GM. Originality/value To the best of the authors' knowledge, this original article, prepared for submission to the Special Issue on Industry Insights is grounded in authentic professional experience and rigorous domain knowledge, contributing substantive practical implications to the field.

title: Socioeconomic and institutional factors associated with pesticide safety knowledge among vegetable farmers in Central Uttar Pradesh, India
abstract: Introduction Unsafe pesticide handling in vegetable production poses risks to applicators, consumers and ecosystems. This study assessed pesticide safety knowledge and its socioeconomic and institutional correlates among vegetable growers in Central Uttar Pradesh, India. Methods A cross-sectional ex-post facto survey was conducted in 2025 among 320 growers from eight villages in Kannauj and Farrukhabad districts, using structured interviews supplemented by field documentation. Knowledge was assessed using a 38-item test. Nine predictors were examined using multiple linear regression; an observed-variable path representation summarized the same adjusted relationships. Results Mean age was 41.58 years; 78.13% were literate and 55.94% operated holdings below 1 ha. Low, medium and high farming experience comprised 43 (13.44%), 230 (71.88%) and 47 (14.69%) growers, respectively. Medium knowledge predominated (65.31%), followed by low (17.50%) and high (17.19%). Regression explained 35.6% of knowledge-score variance (adjusted R 2 = 0.337; F (9, 310) = 19.023, p < 0.001). Education ( B = 0.282, p = 0.006), experience ( B = 0.080, p = 0.012) and information-source score ( B = 0.300, p < 0.001) had positive adjusted associations. Training was not significant ( p = 0.731); 85.31% reported none. The saturated path representation had zero degrees of freedom, precluding meaningful global-fit interpretation. Discussion The findings support evaluating access to credible safety information and training quality and reach. Cross-sectional associations do not establish causation, and interpretation remains subject to predictor-coding and diagnostic limitations.
